meta.label: Video streaming
meta.attribution: Assembled from official pricing pages, terms of service, privacy policies, SEC and other regulatory filings, and platform help centers, not measured data. 'Ownership' scores who controls a service's catalog and what that owner has disclosed about pulling licensed or produced content, not whether you personally hold a copy. Every criterion has a cited basis; reviewed 2026-08. Suggest changes via Contribute.

reads.text: Compare video streaming by privacy, cost, catalog size, and permanence.

axes.label: Cost or overall fit
axes.question: Lower cost or a stronger overall fit?

axes.label: Catalog size
axes.question: How much choice do you need?

consumer.axes: Round 8 practical decision dials, with the S4 cost-or-values default where evidence permits.
consumer.budget: Round 8 honest budget eligibility, with S4 refusing to guess missing cost data.
consumer.archetypes: Round 8 computed answer slots matched to available category evidence.
consumer.page: Round 7 personal precedence extended in Round 9 to the shared decision page for every live category.

criteria.label: Permanence (does what you pay for stay there)

products.name: Netflix
products.description: The largest paid subscription service by revenue, with tiers from an ad-supported plan to a 4K Premium plan. Netflix's own SEC filing describes licensed content as available only for a contractual window, so parts of the catalog change over time.

economical.note: Netflix's official pricing page lists Standard with ads at $8.99/month, Standard at $19.99/month and Premium at $26.99/month in the US, with the old ad-free Basic plan discontinued.

privacy.note: Netflix's privacy statement says it collects information about ads viewed and interacted with, device and IP data, and household inferences, and may disclose personal information to 'Advertising Companies' to select and measure ads, while using contractual and technical measures to keep specific title selections from those marketing partners.

permanence.note: Netflix's 2025 Form 10-K says it amortizes licensed and produced content assets 'over the shorter of each title's contractual window of availability, estimated period of use or ten years,' meaning licensed titles are only guaranteed for a fixed window, not permanently.

accessibility.note: Netflix's own 2016 launch announcement says it went live in 'more than 130 new countries,' bringing its reach to about 190 countries, with China, Crimea, North Korea and Syria excluded; its 2025 Form 10-K still describes the business as entertaining audiences 'across different countries, cultures, languages and tastes.'

products.name: Amazon Prime Video
products.description: Bundled with an Amazon Prime membership or sold as a standalone ad-supported subscription, with an extra fee for the ad-free Prime Video Ultra tier. The FTC found Amazon used deceptive designs to enroll and retain Prime members, and Amazon's own terms say downloaded and even purchased titles can stop being available.

economical.note: Amazon's official announcement says the standalone Prime Video plan with ads costs $8.99/month, and Prime Video Ultra, the ad-free tier with 4K/Dolby Atmos, costs an extra $4.99/month with no change to the base Prime membership price.

privacy.note: Prime Video's Terms of Use say the service 'may provide Amazon with information relating to your use... including information related to the Digital Content that you download and stream... such as whether and when you viewed the Digital Content,' and that some subscriber viewing history may be shared with content providers in a form 'not identifiable to you' unless authorized.

permanence.note: Prime Video's Terms of Use say Amazon 'may automatically remove Digital Content from your Compatible Device after the end of its Viewing Period,' and that even purchased content 'may become unavailable due to potential content provider licensing restrictions or for other reasons.'

accessibility.note: The FTC's order against Amazon found the company 'enrolled millions of consumers in Prime subscriptions without their consent, and knowingly made it difficult for consumers to cancel,' using 'confusing and deceptive user interfaces'; Amazon paid a $1 billion penalty and $1.5 billion in consumer refunds and must now show a clear button to decline Prime.

products.name: Disney+
products.description: Disney's flagship service, now sold in the US mainly as a bundle with Hulu rather than as a plain standalone plan. Disney's own SEC filing for mid-2023 describes a deliberate removal of produced content from its direct-to-consumer platforms, tied to a $2.4 billion impairment charge.

economical.note: Disney's own plans page lists the cheapest current route to Disney+ in the US as the Disney+, Hulu Bundle at $12.99/month with ads, or $19.99/month for the ad-free Bundle Premium; no separate standalone Disney+ price is shown on that page.

privacy.note: California's Attorney General found Disney's opt-out tools only stopped data sharing on the specific device or service used, that its webform did not stop sharing with third-party ad-tech partners, and that Global Privacy Control signals were honored only per device; Disney paid $2.75 million, the largest CCPA penalty to date.

permanence.note: Disney's Form 10-Q for the quarter ended July 1, 2023 says that 'during the third quarter of fiscal 2023, we removed content from our DTC services and terminated certain third-party license agreements,' recording a $2.4 billion Content Impairment Charge, of which $2.0 billion was the write-off of produced content.

accessibility.note: Disney's plans page sells Disney+ across several bundle tiers with ads or ad-free, alongside Hulu, ESPN and HBO Max add-ons, indicating broad mainstream distribution through one consumer signup flow.

products.name: Max
products.description: Warner Bros. Discovery's service, renamed from HBO Max and back again, now live in more than 100 markets. The company's own 2022 SEC filing disclosed billions of dollars in content impairment and write-offs tied to removing licensed and produced titles after its merger.

economical.note: HBO Max's official help center lists three US plans: Basic with Ads at $10.99/month, Standard at $18.49/month and Premium at $22.99/month, each with a 16% discount for annual billing.

privacy.note: HBO Max's own help page says 'We personalize some ad experiences on HBO Max,' and directs users to the Warner Bros. Discovery Privacy Center to manage ad choices and submit Do Not Sell or Share requests.

permanence.note: Warner Bros. Discovery's own Form 8-K disclosed 'strategic content programming assessments, leading to content impairment and development write-offs, of approximately $2.0-$2.5 billion' as part of restructuring after its 2022 merger.

accessibility.note: Warner Bros. Discovery's own pressroom says HBO Max is 'streaming in over 100 markets worldwide,' with launches in early 2026 covering Italy, Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Liechtenstein, Israel and Greece, and further UK and Ireland availability the same year.

products.name: Hulu
products.description: Disney-owned and limited to the United States and its territories. Hulu titles were among those pulled in Disney's 2023 content removal, and Hulu is increasingly sold as part of a Disney+ bundle rather than as a standalone plan.

economical.note: Disney's own site lists the cheapest current route to Hulu in the US as the Disney+, Hulu Bundle at $12.99/month with ads, or $19.99/month for the ad-free Bundle Premium.

privacy.note: California's Attorney General settlement covers Disney account opt-out failures 'across all devices and streaming services associated with consumers' Disney accounts,' which includes Hulu as a Disney-owned service; Disney paid $2.75 million to resolve the case.

permanence.note: Disney's Form 10-Q for the quarter ended July 1, 2023 says Disney 'removed content from our DTC services,' the same content impairment event reported at the time to include titles pulled from both Disney+ and Hulu.

accessibility.note: Hulu is licensed to stream only within the United States and its territories; it has never offered a normal international signup, which limits who can subscribe at all compared with services sold worldwide.

products.name: Apple TV+
products.description: Apple's original-content subscription, sold on its own or inside Apple One, and included free for a period with some new devices. Apple's own media terms reserve the right to remove content, including purchases, if its distribution rights lapse.

economical.note: Apple's own Apple TV+ page lists the price as $12.99/month after a 7-day free trial, with an Apple One bundle starting at $19.95/month.

privacy.note: Apple's own privacy page for the Apple TV app says it uses 'information about the movies and TV shows you purchase and download to offer advertising' on other Apple surfaces, but also states users 'can choose to turn off Personalized Ads.'

permanence.note: Apple's Media Services Terms and Conditions say 'Content also may be removed from our Services at any time (for instance, because Apple loses its right from the Content provider to make it available), after which it cannot be downloaded, redownloaded, or otherwise accessed from Apple,' and that this can apply even to purchased content.

accessibility.note: Apple's own newsroom says the Apple TV app, which carries Apple TV+, is available in 'over 100 countries and regions' across a wide range of devices including non-Apple smart TVs, Roku and Fire TV.

products.name: Paramount+
products.description: Paramount's service carrying CBS, Comedy Central, MTV, Nickelodeon and Showtime titles, sold in dozens of countries. Paramount's own site describes the library only as 'thousands' of episodes and movies rather than giving an exact count.

economical.note: Paramount's own site lists plans starting at $8.99/month for the ad-supported Essential tier, with Premium (ad-free, with Showtime) at $13.99/month.

accessibility.note: Paramount's own site describes the library as 'thousands of full episodes from BET, CBS, Comedy Central, MTV, Nickelodeon, VH1, and more,' and Paramount's global-expansion page describes rolling the service out market by market, including deals in Italy, Germany, Switzerland, Austria, France and South Korea.

products.name: Peacock
products.description: NBCUniversal's service, available only in the United States and its territories. A licensing deal puts a Peacock-branded destination inside Sky's platform in the UK and Europe, but that is Sky content, not a standalone Peacock subscription abroad.

economical.note: Peacock's own help article says Peacock Premium costs '$10.99 a month (+tax) or $109.99 per year (+tax)' and Peacock Premium Plus costs '$16.99 a month (+tax) or $169.99 per year (+tax).'

permanence.note: Comcast's Form 10-K says 'We capitalize the costs of licensed content when the license period begins, the content is made available for use and the costs of the licenses are known. Licensed content is amortized as the associated programs are used,' meaning titles on Peacock are tied to a fixed license period rather than held indefinitely.

accessibility.note: Comcast's own press release describes Peacock content becoming available to 'Sky TV customers and NOW Entertainment Members' as 'a new Peacock destination' inside Sky's existing service, distinct from a direct international Peacock subscription; Peacock itself remains sold only in the US and its territories.

products.name: YouTube
products.description: Free with ads for anyone, with user uploads rather than a licensed studio catalog, plus an optional ad-free Premium tier. Google and YouTube paid a record $170 million to settle FTC and New York allegations that YouTube collected children's data without consent to target ads.

economical.note: YouTube can be watched with ads at no cost; no signup or payment is required to view most public videos.

privacy.note: The FTC's press release says Google and YouTube paid a record $170 million (including a $136 million FTC penalty, the largest COPPA penalty on record) to settle allegations that YouTube 'collected personal information... from viewers of child-directed channels, without first notifying parents and getting their consent,' using the data to 'deliver targeted ads.'

accessibility.note: YouTube is reachable through a web browser or app with no account required for most viewing, and Google's own privacy policy describes using activity data 'across Google services' including YouTube, indicating broad default access.

products.name: Tubi
products.description: A Fox-owned free ad-supported service with no paid subscription option. Its own privacy policy says that sharing viewing data with advertising partners for targeted ads 'could be considered selling' under some state privacy laws, even though Tubi says it does not sell data as defined under others.

economical.note: Tubi's own corporate site describes itself as a free, ad-supported service with no subscription fee.

privacy.note: Tubi's privacy policy says it collects viewing and search history and uses it 'to deliver and measure more relevant, personalized ads,' and states 'we and our advertising partners use certain Personal Data to deliver online advertisements to you on your devices tailored to your interests, which could be considered "selling" under other state privacy laws,' while saying it does not sell data as defined under Virginia's law.

accessibility.note: Tubi's own corporate page says it is available in the US, Canada, Mexico, LATAM, the United Kingdom and Australia, and can be accessed on 'over 30 devices.'

products.name: Pluto TV
products.description: A free, ad-supported live-channel and on-demand service owned by Paramount. Paramount's own press page calls it 'a global leader in free streaming television,' built on partnerships with hundreds of media companies rather than a paid catalog.

economical.note: Pluto TV's own site describes itself as letting people 'Watch 1000s of free movies and TV shows on demand & 100s of live TV channels for free,' with no subscription fee.

catalog.note: Pluto TV's own site says it offers '1000s of free movies and TV shows on demand & 100s of live TV channels,' a broad but imprecise figure compared with services that publish an exact title count.

accessibility.note: Paramount's own press page describes Pluto TV as 'the leading free streaming television service' and 'a global leader in free streaming television,' built in partnership with 'over 425 international media companies.'

products.name: Plex
products.description: A free ad-supported film and TV library plus a self-hosted media server for files you already own. Plex's own privacy policy says it will not collect or sell information about titles in a personal media library, while it does share some account data for advertising on the free streaming side.

economical.note: Plex's own free-movies page says its on-demand movies and shows are '100% Free' and fully licensed, with no credit card required, and the Plex Media Server software is also free to run.

privacy.note: Plex's March 2025 privacy policy states 'We do not and will not collect information about content or titles in your personal media library or what you've played,' and for personal media users specifically, 'we do NOT, and will not, share or sell any information about the content and titles on or your use of a personal media server,' while separately listing hashed emails and online identifiers as data shared with advertisers for the ad-supported streaming side.

catalog.note: Plex's own free-movies page says it offers 'Stream 50K+ titles on demand' plus '600+ channels' of free live TV.

permanence.note: Plex's Terms of Service for the Plex Media Server say the software may only be used on 'a device or hardware that you own' and that 'Content available on your PMS Software must be on storage that you own,' meaning the self-hosted side of Plex is explicitly built around content you already control.

accessibility.note: The free streaming catalog requires no payment and no account beyond signup, while running a personal Plex Media Server requires setting up and maintaining your own hardware, a materially higher effort than opening an app.

products.name: Kanopy
products.description: A film library available at no direct cost through a participating public library card, funded by the library rather than by a subscription or ads. Access is rationed by a monthly ticket allowance rather than by price.

economical.note: The San Francisco Public Library's own FAQ says Kanopy 'is free to San Francisco Public Library cardholders,' with the library paying for access on the cardholder's behalf.

catalog.note: The San Francisco Public Library's own FAQ describes Kanopy as providing access to 'more than 30,000 independent and documentary films,' including Criterion Collection and Great Courses titles.

accessibility.note: The San Francisco Public Library's own FAQ says a valid library card and PIN are required, and that cardholders 'receive 30 tickets to use every month,' with most titles costing a minimum of 2 tickets and unused tickets not carrying over.

products.name: Criterion Channel
products.description: The Criterion Collection's own hand-picked subscription, limited to the United States and Canada, built around a rotating library of about 2,000 films plus shorts and supplements rather than a broad mainstream catalog.

economical.note: Criterion's own FAQ says 'A monthly subscription to the Criterion Channel costs $10.99 USD a month and an annual subscription costs $99.99 USD a year,' with a free 7-day trial.

catalog.note: Criterion's own FAQ says subscribers 'can browse and filter the 2000+ films available to stream,' along with 'more than 500 shorts and 5,000 supplementary features.'

accessibility.note: Criterion's own FAQ says 'The Criterion Channel is available only in the U.S. and Canada,' with no wider international launch yet, and there is no free ad-supported tier.

products.name: Mubi
products.description: A hand-picked subscription built around a daily rotation: films are added to the main selection and depart on a schedule, with Mubi's own help center flagging departures roughly two weeks ahead.

economical.note: Mubi's own membership page lists the standard MUBI plan at $14.99/month or $119.88/year, with a pricier MUBI GO tier at $19.99/month that adds a weekly cinema ticket in select cities.

permanence.note: Mubi's own help center says 'we will always label films that are leaving the platform within the next 14 days,' confirming that films are only available on Mubi for a limited, rotating window rather than staying indefinitely.

accessibility.note: Mubi's own membership page and App Store listing note that content and pricing vary by country but do not give a full list of served countries; the base subscription is sold with no free ad-supported tier.

products.name: Internet Archive (public domain and open film collections)
products.description: The nonprofit Internet Archive's public-domain and openly licensed film collections, free to stream or download with no purchase. The Archive says it does not charge for access, sell user data, or run ads.

economical.note: The Internet Archive's own site states it does not 'charge for access, sell user information, or run ads,' and is 'powered by online donations' rather than fees.

privacy.note: The Internet Archive's own privacy statement says it does not 'charge for access, sell user information, or run ads,' and separately says of donor data, 'We do not sell or trade your information with anyone.'

catalog.note: The Archive's 'Public Domain Movies' collection page lists 385 files totalling 971.6GB in this single named collection; the Archive hosts several other separate film collections beyond this one, so this figure describes one collection rather than the whole site.

permanence.note: The Archive describes itself as an independent nonprofit funded by donations rather than ad revenue or licensing deals, and its film holdings are public domain or rights-cleared for redistribution, so titles are not subject to the kind of licensing-window removal that Netflix, Disney and Warner Bros. Discovery disclose in their own filings.

accessibility.note: The Public Domain Movies collection page is titled 'Free Download, Borrow, and Streaming,' and offers multiple downloadable formats without a purchase or subscription.
